module_name: Ubiquitin-Regulated MAPK Signaling in Cancer and Inflammation
summary: This module centers on the functional integration of the MAPK signaling cascade and the ubiquitin-mediated proteolysis system, which collectively govern critical cellular processes such as proliferation, differentiation, migration, and inflammatory responses. The gene set is functionally grouped into two interconnected axes: (1) a broad network of serine/threonine kinases (e.g., RAF family, MAPK1/3, MAPK8/9/10/14, AKT1/2/3, CDKs, GSK3, and AMPK subunits) that propagate mitogenic and stress signals, and (2) a comprehensive ubiquitin machinery including E1/E2 enzymes, cullin-RBX scaffolds, APC/C subunits, and specific E3 ligases (e.g., SMURF1, DTL, Parkin, NEDD4, Cbl, MDM2, COP1). This architecture enables precise post-translational control of signaling node stability, receptor internalization, and downstream transcription factor activity. Literature strongly supports the clinical relevance of this crosstalk: in lung cancer, the E3 ligase DTL mediates PDCD4 ubiquitination to modulate MAPK/JNK signaling and drive tumor malignancy; in hepatocellular carcinoma, circCCNY scaffolds SMURF1 to promote HSP60 degradation, thereby activating RKIP and suppressing the MAPK/c-Myc/PD-L1 axis to overcome lenvatinib resistance. Additionally, MAPK pathway modulation via ubiquitin-dependent mechanisms has been implicated in diabetes cardiomyopathy (p38MAPK/AKT/FOS regulation) and inflammatory conditions, underscoring this module as a central regulatory hub and multi-disease therapeutic target.

module_name: DNA Replication and Cell Cycle Progression Regulated by BCR/MAPK Signaling
summary: This module centers on DNA replication initiation and cell cycle progression, tightly coordinated by upstream signaling cascades including BCR and MAPK pathways. The gene set encompasses the core replisome and licensing machinery (ORC1-6, MCM2-7, GINS, CDC45, CDK2, CDC7/DBF4, PCNA, RPA, and DNA polymerases α/δ/ε), alongside chromatin remodelers (clustered and variant histones) and the 26S/20S proteasome system, which collectively ensure genome duplication, chromatin dynamics, and protein homeostasis. Functionally, BCR signaling complexes (CD79A/B, SYK, BLNK, PI3K, PLCG2) and MAPK modules converge on critical proliferative nodes (RAS, AKT, NF-κB, and calcium signaling), which phosphorylate replication initiators, drive S-phase entry, and maintain cell survival. Literature underscores the clinical relevance of this network: in malignant lymphoid cells, HDAC10 preserves replication fidelity by regulating MYC-dependent POLD1 expression, while S-CDK-mediated phosphorylation of Mcm10 is essential for CMG helicase activation and S-phase progression. Additionally, ORC-deficient cancer cells demonstrate that excess MCM2-7 licensing can persist through alternative genomic cues, highlighting adaptive replication mechanisms in oncogenesis. Concurrently, axes like MSTN/PSMA6/AKT-mTOR illustrate how signaling networks modulate both replication-coupled proliferation and terminal differentiation. Together, these pathways form a cohesive regulatory hub linking extracellular and immune cues to genomic stability and cell cycle control, with significant implications for hematological malignancies and proliferative disorders.

module_name: Mitochondrial Oxidative Phosphorylation and Metabolic-Signaling Integration in Disease
summary: This module centers on mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) and the citrate cycle as core drivers of cellular energy metabolism, intricately coordinated with MAPK cascade, T cell receptor signaling, and protein ubiquitination pathways. Key genes include mitochondrial respiratory chain subunits (NDUFA, COX, ATP5, UQCRC families), TCA cycle enzymes (IDH, SDH, OGDH, PDH), MAPK/TCR signaling components (RAF, MAPK, CD3, CD28, LCK, FYN, GRB2), and the ubiquitin-proteasome system (UBB, UBE2, USP, RNF families) that regulate protein turnover, signaling fidelity, and metabolic adaptation. Literature highlights the critical role of OXPHOS dysregulation across multiple disease contexts: elevated mitochondrial respiration and COX activity promote vascular calcification in chronic kidney disease and drive everolimus resistance in breast cancer, while targeted suppression of OXPHOS (e.g., via NDUFA7 downregulation) induces ROS-mediated apoptosis in colorectal cancer. Additionally, mitochondrial complex I and ATP synthesis genes are implicated in major psychiatric disorders, underscoring how metabolic and signaling networks converge to regulate cellular fate, immune responses, and therapeutic vulnerability.

module_name: Replicative DNA Polymerase and Primosome Complex in Cell Proliferation and Metabolic Regulation
summary: This module centers on the molecular machinery governing DNA replication initiation and transcription-replication coordination. The core functional cluster comprises the DNA polymerase alpha:primase complex (POLA1, POLA2, PRIM1, PRIM2) and multiple subunits of DNA polymerase epsilon (POLE, POLE2, POLE3, POLE4), which collectively catalyze RNA-DNA primer synthesis and nascent strand elongation. These replicative enzymes operate in concert with transcriptional elongation and chromatin remodeling factors, including CDK9, CCNT2, and SPT6, to synchronize genomic duplication with gene expression programs essential for cell cycle progression and tissue differentiation. Literature insights highlight the structural and dynamic requirements of the primosome, with recent cryoEM studies detailing the conformational transitions of PRIM1, PRIM2, and POLA1 during primer handover. Concurrently, the presence of metabolic and signaling components—such as IGF2 and mitochondrial 3-oxoacyl-ACP synthase—alongside short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) biosynthetic pathways, suggests a regulatory cross-talk where metabolic cues and growth factors modulate replicative and differentiative states. IGF2 has been linked to tissue remodeling and gastrointestinal function, while SCFA metabolism influences systemic signaling that can impact cell differentiation and neuromuscular physiology. Collectively, this module integrates DNA replication initiation, transcriptional regulation, and metabolic signaling to orchestrate coordinated cellular proliferation and differentiation.

module_name: Immune Cell Activation, Antigen Presentation, and Inflammatory Signaling
summary: This module encapsulates the coordinated activation of innate and adaptive immunity, centered on antigen presentation, lymphocyte receptor signaling, and inflammatory cytokine networks. Key genes include major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class I and II molecules, co-stimulatory markers (CD80, CD86, CD274), T cell receptor (TCR) and B cell receptor (BCR) components, diverse interleukins and chemokines/receptors (CXCR5, CCR family), complement system proteins, and apoptotic regulators like Fas. Literature insights underscore this immune-centric architecture: CXCR5hi B cells and dendritic cells promote hepatic inflammation and antitumor responses via enhanced MHC-II and CD80/CD86 expression; FTO-mediated m6A modification stabilizes Fas mRNA to regulate CD8+ T cell survival; and severe infectious or metabolic-inflammatory conditions (e.g., pneumonia, MASH, SARS-CoV-2) trigger robust upregulation of pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α) and chemokines (CCL5), highlighting the module's critical role in host defense, immunoregulation, and disease progression.

module_name: Ubiquitin-Dependent Coordination of DNA Replication and Lipid Metabolism
summary: This module centers on the ubiquitin-proteasome system's role in dynamically coordinating DNA replication, cell cycle progression, and de novo fatty acid biosynthesis. The replisome and DNA repair machinery (MCM complex, DNA polymerases α/δ/ε, PCNA, RFC, RPA, FEN1, and DNA ligase 1) are tightly regulated by a massive network of E3 ubiquitin ligases (CUL4-DDB1, MARCH2, TRIM, F-box, and HECT families) and E2 conjugating enzymes, which control protein turnover to ensure replication fidelity and cell cycle transitions. Concurrently, the module encompasses core lipogenic enzymes (FASN, ACCα/β, ACSL family, and malonyl-CoA-ACP transacylase) that drive membrane biosynthesis required for proliferating cells. Literature highlights the functional intersection of these pathways: MARCH2-mediated ubiquitination targets fatty acid synthase (FASN) for proteasomal degradation, modulating hepatic lipid homeostasis and mitigating metabolic dysfunction-associated fatty liver disease (MAFLD). Similarly, CUL4-based E3 ligase complexes maintain proteostasis of DNA replication and ciliary proteins during developmental cycles, while cell cycle regulators like DSCC1 and CDK2 integrate replication fork dynamics with DNA damage response pathways. Collectively, these components illustrate a unified regulatory network where ubiquitin-dependent proteolysis balances nucleic acid synthesis, lipid metabolism, and genomic stability in response to metabolic cues, proliferative demands, and environmental stress.

module_name: Adaptive Immune Activation and Lymphocyte Receptor Signaling
summary: This module encapsulates the coordinated signaling cascade driving adaptive immunity, primarily centered on T cell receptor (TCR) and B cell receptor (BCR) activation, modulated by costimulatory checkpoints and antigen presentation. Key functional clusters include the antigen-recognition complexes (TCR/CD3, BCR/CD79, MHC class I/II, and CD1 molecules), proximal tyrosine kinases (LCK, FYN, SYK, BTK, JAKs), and downstream second-messenger systems (G proteins, adenylate cyclases, phospholipases C/D/A2, and voltage-gated/inward-rectifying ion channels) that translate receptor engagement into calcium flux and cAMP dynamics. Costimulatory and inhibitory receptors (CD28, CTLA-4, ICOS, PD-1, CD80/86, CD274) precisely regulate the activation threshold to prevent autoimmunity or enable robust pathogen clearance. Transcription factors (NFAT, NF-κB, AP-1) and effector cytokines (IL-2, IL-4, IL-17, IFNs) execute lineage-specific differentiation and immune effector functions. Recent literature underscores the genetic architecture of this module, with eQTL studies identifying regulatory variants in SYK, VAV2, and PLCG2 that modulate BCR signaling and adaptive immune outcomes. Furthermore, research highlights how dendritic cell maturation markers (MHC-II, CD86) dictate T cell activation capacity, while HLA-peptide specificity and restricted TCR clonality drive autoreactive responses in autoimmune conditions like ANCA vasculitis. Although the module includes components typically associated with neuronal signaling (e.g., glutamate receptors, GPCRs), these primarily represent conserved second-messenger and scaffold networks co-opted by lymphocytes for rapid signal transduction, calcium homeostasis, and metabolic reprogramming during immune activation.

module_name: Ubiquitin-Proteasome-Mediated Apoptosis and Immune Inflammatory Signaling
summary: This module centers on the tightly regulated network governing programmed cell death and immune/inflammatory responses, heavily modulated by protein homeostasis mechanisms and kinase signaling cascades. The collective gene set spans the intrinsic and extrinsic apoptotic pathways (BCL2 family regulators, caspases 1–12, FAS/FASLG, TRAIL receptors, PERFORIN/GZMB), the ubiquitin-proteasome system (26S/20S proteasome subunits, E3 ligases including TRIM/F-box/SMURF families, UBR1/2, and E1/E2 conjugating enzymes), and major signaling hubs (AKT, NF-κB, MAPK/p38/JNK/ERK, ATM/ATR, and PARPs). Immune-related components (MHC I/II, TCR/BCR signaling adaptors, cytokine receptors, and KIR/LILR families) are integrated to reflect antigen processing and lymphocyte regulation. Literature insights strongly support this functional convergence: interventions targeting the Akt/NF-κB and p38 MAPK axes reduce apoptosis and neuroinflammation in Alzheimer’s models, while E3 ligases like UBR1/UBR2 maintain proteostasis and modulate ER stress-induced apoptosis via the N-degron pathway. In diabetic acute kidney injury, pharmacological suppression of the PERK/CHOP/NF-κB axis mitigates ER stress and apoptotic damage. Additionally, immune cell-specific regulators (e.g., FEM1B) enhance TRAIL-mediated extrinsic apoptosis through caspase-8/3 activation, and natural compounds (e.g., Ashwagandha) alleviate stress-induced apoptosis and inflammatory cytokine release in depression models. Collectively, the module represents a critical regulatory hub where proteasomal degradation, kinase-mediated phosphorylation, and apoptotic execution intersect to control cellular fate, immune surveillance, and tissue homeostasis across diverse pathological states.

module_name: Apoptosis and MAPK Signaling in Cellular Stress and Cancer
summary: This module centers on the integrated regulation of apoptosis and the MAPK signaling cascade, which collectively govern cell fate in response to physiological stress, growth factor signaling, and therapeutic interventions. Key functional groups include the apoptotic executioners and regulators (caspases, BCL2 family proteins, IAPs, FAS/TRAIL receptors), the MAPK cascade components (ERK, JNK, p38, RAF/MEK/MAP3Ks, RAS), and stress/DNA damage sensors (ATM, TP53, PARPs). Literature highlights the clinical relevance of this crosstalk: matrine mitigates cellular senescence by downregulating p38/JNK/ERK and PI3K/Akt signaling while suppressing CASP3 and senescence markers; Evofosfamide exploits hypoxia to trigger caspase-3/7-dependent apoptosis and PARP cleavage in breast cancer; in AML, Dasatinib overcomes BCL2 inhibitor resistance by degrading MCL1 and promoting caspase-3 activation; quercetin reverses cisplatin resistance in ovarian cancer by suppressing MAPK-driven MMP1 expression; and icaritin induces caspase-independent paraptosis via BHLHE40-mediated ER stress and mitochondrial dysfunction. Together, these pathways illustrate a dynamic network where kinase signaling and apoptotic checkpoints converge to modulate disease progression, therapeutic response, and cellular homeostasis.

module_name: Regulation of Striated Muscle Cell Differentiation and Satellite Cell Fate
summary: This module centers on the integrated signaling, epigenetic, and apoptotic networks that govern striated muscle cell differentiation and satellite cell fate determination, encompassing both positive and negative regulatory mechanisms. Core growth factor signaling is driven by IGF2, IGFBP5, and AKT1, which promote myogenic progression through the PI3K/AKT/mTOR axis, while TGF-β/BMP pathway members (BMPR1A, BMPR2, SMAD1, ID2) provide counter-regulatory or fine-tuning signals during muscle development. Transcriptional and chromatin-remodeling regulators such as HDAC9, EZH2, ZBED6, SPT6, and YBX1 orchestrate epigenetic reprogramming essential for myogenic commitment. Apoptotic checkpoints (CASP3, CASP7) and differentiation-associated kinases (MAPK14, CAMK1) balance cell survival with terminal differentiation, while muscle-specific effectors like POPDC family members and myotrophin modulate calcium signaling and excitation-contraction coupling during myogenesis. Literature strongly supports this cohesive framework: MSTN and PSMA6-mediated epigenetic remodeling (via TET2) directly regulate AKT/mTOR signaling and satellite cell differentiation in bovine skeletal muscle. TNFα deficiency has been shown to enhance myogenesis by altering IGF2 and CASP7 distribution, promoting MyoD targets and regenerative capacity. Furthermore, exosome-mediated CASP3 targeting and epigenetic factors like ZBED6 are implicated in muscle adaptation and tendon-muscle unit development. Together, these elements form a tightly coordinated module where growth factor signaling, BMP/TGF-β modulation, epigenetic reprogramming, and controlled apoptosis converge to direct skeletal muscle development, satellite cell specification, and regenerative capacity.

module_name: Ubiquitin-Proteasome System and Proteasomal Degradation in Disease
summary: This module centers on the ubiquitin-proteasome system (UPS), a highly coordinated regulatory network governing selective protein degradation and cellular homeostasis. The system operates through a sequential enzymatic cascade: E1 ubiquitin-activating enzymes prime ubiquitin, which is transferred to a diverse array of E2 ubiquitin-conjugating enzymes (e.g., UBE2C, UBE2D, UBE2T, UBE2Z), and finally handed off to substrate-specific E3 ubiquitin ligases. The E3 ligases, encompassing Cullin-RING, HECT, RBR, F-box, and RING-finger families (including SMURF2, NEDD4, TRAFs, and APC/C components), dictate target recognition and chain topology. This conjugation process is dynamically counterbalanced by deubiquitinating enzymes (DUBs) such as USP5, USP7, and OTUD5, which reverse tagging to fine-tune protein stability. The 26S proteasome complex then executes ATP-dependent degradation of polyubiquitinated substrates, playing critical roles in cell cycle progression, DNA repair, immune signaling, and apoptosis. Recent literature underscores the pathological and therapeutic relevance of this network: SMURF2-mediated ubiquitination and degradation of AXIN1 drives cardiac hypertrophy via Wnt/β-catenin signaling, a process reversible by the inhibitor heclin. In oncology, USP5 stabilizes EphA2 to confer nasopharyngeal carcinoma radioresistance, while the E3 ligase Pirh2 targets the RNA-binding protein HuR for proteasomal clearance, modulating c-Myc expression and heat-shock survival. Furthermore, branched ubiquitin chain dynamics (K29/K48) regulated by OTUD5 and E3 ligases like TRIP12 and UBR5 dictate TNF-α/NF-κB signaling and osteoporosis progression. In neurodegeneration, the SPHK2/S1P pathway modulates neuronal ubiquitination networks involving HUWE1 and UBE2Z, linking UPS dysfunction to Huntington’s disease. Collectively, this module demonstrates how precise spatiotemporal control of ubiquitin conjugation, deconjugation, and proteasomal clearance orchestrates fundamental cellular processes and serves as a central therapeutic node across cancer, cardiovascular remodeling, neurodegeneration, and immune dysregulation.

module_name: Glutamatergic Synaptic Transmission and Plasticity in Neurodevelopmental Disorders
summary: This module encapsulates the core mechanisms of excitatory neurotransmission and synaptic plasticity in the central nervous system, primarily driven by glutamatergic signaling. Functionally, it integrates glutamate receptor activation (spanning NMDA, AMPA, kainate, and metabotropic subtypes) with downstream G-protein and calcium signaling cascades, synaptic scaffolding complexes (including DLG, Homer, and MAGUK family proteins), and presynaptic vesicle trafficking and cytoskeletal dynamics (mediated by RAB GTPases, synapsins, and actin regulators). Literature reveals that precise regulation of this module is critical for normal neurodevelopment, with its dysregulation strongly implicated in autism spectrum disorder (ASD), intellectual disability, and ADHD. For instance, mutations in the RhoGEF Trio or haploinsufficiency of SYNGAP1 disrupt Neuroligin-1-mediated synaptogenesis and NMDA receptor maturation, leading to aberrant excitatory signaling and cognitive/behavioral deficits. Similarly, ADHD-associated variants in ADGRL3 and GABAergic disruptions (e.g., Gabrb1 loss) indirectly hyperactivate glutamatergic pathways, shifting the excitation-inhibition balance and altering astrocytic glutamate-glutamine cycling. Furthermore, in Alzheimer’s disease models, neuroimmune interactions modulate glutamatergic synaptic gene expression, underscoring the module’s broader role in maintaining synaptic homeostasis across neurodevelopmental and neurodegenerative contexts.

module_name: Eukaryotic DNA Replication Licensing, Fork Progression, and Genomic Stability
summary: This module encompasses the coordinated molecular machinery and regulatory networks governing eukaryotic DNA replication initiation, elongation, and cell cycle progression. The process begins with pre-replication complex (pre-RC) licensing during G1, driven by the origin recognition complex (ORC1-6), CDC6, and the MCM2-7 helicase. Upon S-phase entry, CDK2 and DBF4-CDC7 kinase activation triggers MCM unwinding, recruiting DNA polymerases (POLα/δ/ε), PCNA sliding clamps, RFC loaders, and RPA for leading and lagging strand synthesis. Okazaki fragment maturation is completed by FEN1 and RNase H1, followed by DNA ligase I. Tight regulation prevents re-replication and genomic instability through proteasome-dependent degradation of chromatin-bound ORC6, GEMIN1-mediated MCM inhibition, and APC/C-driven cyclin turnover. Literature highlights the clinical relevance of this module: proteasome-mediated clearance of ORC6 safeguards against aberrant MCM reloading and tetraploidy, directly linking replication control to cancer prevention (PubMed:40554748). MCM2 and MCM6 are central to replication initiation and are implicated in hepatocellular carcinoma progression and breast cancer chemosensitivity, where replication stress and DNA damage repair intersect with oncogenic signaling (PubMed:40186059, 38117512). Furthermore, dynamic tracking of ORC1, MCM6, and PCNA reveals their critical roles in normal development and placental function, with dysregulation correlating with DNA damage markers and metabolic stress (PubMed:40507884, 39900600). Collectively, this module illustrates how precise spatiotemporal control of replication factors maintains genomic integrity, with failures directly contributing to tumorigenesis, aneuploidy, and developmental disorders.

module_name: Mitochondrial Oxidative Phosphorylation and Electron Transport Chain Dynamics
summary: This module centers on mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) and the electron transport chain (ETC), representing a highly coordinated bioenergetic system that converts metabolic reducing equivalents into cellular ATP. The genes are functionally grouped into three interconnected axes: (1) Core respiratory complexes (I–IV) and ATP synthase (Complex V), which form the structural and catalytic backbone of proton pumping and ATP generation; (2) Electron transfer and redox regulation modules, including electron transfer flavoproteins, ferredoxins, cytochrome c, and assembly factors (e.g., COX10, COX15, COX17), which ensure efficient electron flux and complex biogenesis; and (3) Metabolic dehydrogenases and reductases (e.g., isocitrate/malic dehydrogenases, aldo-keto reductases, glutathione system), which feed NAD(P)H into the ETC while maintaining redox homeostasis. Recent literature consistently highlights the centrality of this module in disease pathogenesis. In primary open-angle glaucoma, endothelin-1 downregulates critical ETC components like COX17 and ATP5H, impairing ATP synthesis and driving retinal ganglion cell apoptosis. In metabolic dysregulation, berberine restores glucose/lipid homeostasis by selectively modulating Complex I abundance via SIRT3-dependent deacetylation. Furthermore, NOX4-driven mitochondrial ROS disrupts OXPHOS in aging macrophages, forcing a pathological shift toward glycolysis and promoting a pro-inflammatory phenotype that accelerates atherosclerosis. Similarly, in Down syndrome, elevated NOX4 and defective ETC function impair the developmental transition from glycolysis to oxidative phosphorylation during neural differentiation. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that precise regulation of mitochondrial electron transfer and ATP synthesis is essential for cellular bioenergetics, and its dysfunction serves as a unifying mechanism across neurodegenerative, metabolic, cardiovascular, and developmental diseases.

module_name: Adaptive Immune Receptor Signaling and Lymphocyte Activation
summary: This module centers on the coordinated signaling networks that drive adaptive immunity, primarily through T-cell receptor (TCR) and B-cell receptor (BCR) pathways. Genes are functionally grouped into antigen recognition and presentation complexes (MHC class I/II, CD1, TCR/BCR chains, and immunoglobulin regions), intracellular signal transduction machinery (Src-family kinases like LCK/FYN, SYK, BTK, PI3K, PLCγ, VAV GEFs, and MAPK/AKT cascades), co-stimulatory and checkpoint regulators (CD28, CTLA-4, PD-1, ICOS, CD80/CD86, and TNFRSF family members), and downstream effector mediators (IFN, IL, and TNF/TNFSF cytokines with corresponding receptors). These pathways exhibit synergistic and antagonistic crosstalk, where stimulatory signals are balanced by inhibitory checkpoints to maintain peripheral tolerance. Research insights highlight the clinical relevance of this module: reverse vaccinology leverages TLR and MHC interactions to design robust hMPXV vaccines; chronic inflammatory conditions like rheumatoid arthritis and periodontitis exhibit elevated TNF/IFN/IL networks that drive tissue destruction; pathogen recognition via TLR2 mediates age-dependent bone loss in septic arthritis; immune evasion in chronic lymphocytic leukemia involves HLA-G transfer to T cells; and sepsis progression is tightly linked to TNFSF10 expression and PI3K-MAPK dysregulation. Collectively, this module illustrates how adaptive immune receptor signaling integrates pathogen detection, lymphocyte proliferation, and cytokine-driven effector functions, with direct implications for infectious disease, autoimmunity, and cancer immunotherapy.

module_name: De Novo Lipogenesis and TCA Cycle Integration in Metabolic Dysregulation
summary: This module centers on the metabolic crosstalk between the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle and de novo fatty acid biosynthesis, highlighting how mitochondrial citrate export fuels cytosolic lipid production. Key enzymatic drivers include ATP citrate lyase (ACLY), which converts TCA-derived citrate to acetyl-CoA, and acetyl-CoA carboxylases (ACCA/ACCB), which catalyze the rate-limiting formation of malonyl-CoA. Fatty acid synthase (FASN) and the ELOVL elongase family extend carbon chains, while acyl-CoA synthetases (ACSL/ACSM), desaturases (SCD), and thioesterases fine-tune lipid composition and activation. Metabolic homeostasis is tightly regulated by AMPK signaling and post-transcriptional control, such as miR-125b targeting elongation/degradation enzymes (MECR, ACADS). Literature underscores the clinical and pathological relevance of this axis: viral infections (e.g., VACV) hijack the VGF-EGFR-Akt pathway to phosphorylate ACLY, boosting neutral lipid droplet synthesis for viral replication, while ACLY knockout in yeast severely impairs lipid accumulation. Conversely, dietary interventions targeting this module (e.g., persimmon leaf extract, kudzu resistant starch) ameliorate hyperlipidemia and NAFLD by downregulating FASN, ACC, and SCD1 expression while restoring intestinal short-chain fatty acid balance. Collectively, these pathways form a cohesive metabolic hub linking cellular energy status, membrane biogenesis, and metabolic disease progression.
